events.title: Renewed call for 'blood grain' transit ban in Latvia

articles.text: Renewed call for 'blood grain' transit ban in Latvia Share Follow: Follow LSM on Google Photo: LETA, Ieva Lūka Today, 9:32 Business Authors: LSM English (Latvian Public Media) On November 7th, protesters in Jēkabpils demanded that the transit of Russian grain via Latvia be stopped within 14 days. Their deadline expired on Saturday, November 21. Referring also to the foiled sabotage attempt against an Estonian drone manufacturer, which is to lead to the closure of the Estonian-Russian border, the organizers are now demanding that Latvia follow suit and that the government should completely close Latvia's border with Russia and stop any transit of goods. The demands of the participants of the November 7 protest were addressed to Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (Joint List) and the Cabinet of Ministers. They demanded legally binding decisions to stop the transit of Russian grain, including grain illegally exported from the occupied territories of Ukraine, through Latvian territory, railway infrastructure and ports. The organizers emphasize that the head of government heard the demands of the participants in person and the fulfillment of his promises should be publicly verifiable. As previously reported , in one of her final acts as Foreign Minister, Baiba Braže (New Unity) sent proposals to the government to ban the transit of 'blood grain' from the aggressor states of Russia and Belarus. "We are deeply disappointed in Andris Kulbergs' promises and their fulfillment. In Jēkabpils, we demanded a result - the suspension of transit within 14 days. The political responsibility for the result lies with the government and its leader. In recent weeks, various politicians have repeatedly publicly stated that it is already too late to ban grain transit - we categorically oppose this statement! For the Russians to export all their bloody grain, it is a matter of many months, even years," emphasizes farmer and protest organizer Gundars Kalve. According to the protest organizers, the Foreign Ministry's proposal was not considered, and currently everything indicates that it is no longer on the government's agenda following the installation of a new coalition, while Russian grain is still being transported through Latvia. Meanwhile, Lithuania has reportedly imposed a hold on grain shipments from Russia and Belarus until origin checks are completed. This is not a permanent transit ban, but such an arrangement could delay cargo movements for several months. Additional grounds for tough action, according to the protesters, are the foiled sabotage attempt against the Estonian drone manufacturer "Threod Systems" on the night of November 14. Estonian authorities attribute this to the activities of Russian military intelligence services. As a result of cooperation between Latvian and Estonian security services, eight Latvian nationals have been detained. Following this incident, Estonia announced a plan to close all land border crossings with Russia from December 1. "We demand an immediate decision to completely close Latvia's border with Russia, including stopping any transit of goods. Latvia's security should be the government's priority," Kalve said. The protest organizers will continue their work, he said encouraging public discussions, demanding answers from officials, and regularly informing the public about government decisions and their implementation. On Latvian Radio's "Labrīt" program, Kalve said about the protesters' future plans: "Further action is unclear. First of all, the protest on November 7 was relatively poorly attended, public support was not as we had hoped. A collection of signatures has also been launched on the "manabalss.lv" platform, but there are few signatures so far." Seen a mistake?
